title: [Feature]: Format Conversion for AI-Generated Output — PDF / PPT / Excel Beyond the Existing DOCX-Only Export
body:
## Background

Cherry Studio's only document export today is Word (`.docx`) via the `docx` npm library at `src/main/services/ExportService.ts:367-408`. Every other format users routinely ask for — **PDF, PowerPoint, Excel** — has no conversion path at all. The artifact pane (`ArtifactPane.tsx`) can *preview* PDFs, Excel files, and Word docs, but exposes no "Save as" or "Convert to" affordance. Skills under `resources/skills/` don't fill the gap either. The result is a sharp, repeated production failure observed in the May 2026 enterprise workshop: users ask the Agent for a PPT or PDF report, the Agent produces HTML or markdown (because that's what its tools can emit), and the user is stuck — they can either copy-paste the markdown into an external tool, screenshot the rendered output, or give up. The instructor spent significant class time teaching the workaround "first let the Agent write facts in markdown, you confirm, then *separately* convert to PPT" — which itself fails because there's no convert step in the product. This is the highest-frequency end-of-workflow gap in the V2 product surface, and unlike most preprocessing work it's entirely solvable with battle-tested OSS libraries (`pptxgenjs`, `exceljs`, headless Chromium / `puppeteer` for PDF).

## Goal

Any AI-generated markdown content — from a chat message, an artifact in the artifact pane, or a Note — can be converted to PDF, PowerPoint, Excel, or Word in one click, and the same conversion is available as a tool call the Agent can invoke programmatically so that "give me a PPT" produces a real `.pptx` file end-to-end.

## Spec

- The existing "Export" menu on chat messages is extended from `Word / Image / Markdown / external integrations` to also include **PDF**, **PowerPoint**, and **Excel**. The same menu shape is added to artifacts in the artifact pane and to Notes (Notes only exposed Word + Image + integrations today).
- Format → library mapping:
  - **PDF** → headless Chromium via Electron's built-in `webContents.printToPDF()` (no new dependency). The markdown is rendered using Cherry's existing markdown renderer to ensure visual fidelity with what the user sees in chat.
  - **PPT** → `pptxgenjs` (pure-JS, no Python). Markdown is parsed: each `## H2` becomes a slide; bullets become bullet content; embedded images/tables become slide assets.
  - **Excel** → `exceljs` (pure-JS). Markdown tables become sheets; multiple tables become separate sheets named by surrounding `## H2` headers.
  - **Word** → existing path unchanged.
- All four conversions surface a `loading` toast during conversion (per #15653) and a `success` toast with `Open file` action on completion.
- A new IPC channel `export:convertAndSave(markdown, format, defaultName)` lives in main and dispatches to the appropriate converter.
- The same conversion is exposed as an **Agent tool** (`convert_to_document(markdown, format)`) that any built-in or user-created agent can call. When the user asks an Agent "give me a PPT summary of yesterday's PRs", the Agent uses this tool to produce the actual `.pptx` and attaches it to its response — no manual user step.
- In-chat artifact output: when an Agent returns markdown content via the new tool, the result appears as an attached file in the agent's message (downloadable + previewable), not as inline markdown the user has to manually convert.
- Existing DOCX export continues to use the `docx` library unchanged. PPT/Excel/PDF paths are additive — no regression for the existing flow.
- Provider-specific conversion failures (e.g., a malformed markdown table that can't map to an Excel sheet) surface a typed error toast (per #15651) with `View extracted preview` action so the user sees what went wrong instead of a silent failure.

## Verification

- User right-clicks an Agent's markdown response containing 5 `## H2` sections with bullets and a table → "Export" menu shows `PDF / Word / PowerPoint / Excel / Image / Markdown / Notion / Yuque / ...`. Clicking `PowerPoint` shows a `loading` toast, then a `success` toast `Saved deck.pptx` with `Open file` action. Opening the file: 5 slides, bullets where expected, the table rendered as a slide.
- User clicks `PDF` on the same message → headless Chromium renders the markdown via Cherry's renderer; produced PDF visually matches the in-chat appearance (same fonts, code highlighting, table formatting).
- User clicks `Excel` on a message containing 3 markdown tables under `## Revenue`, `## Expenses`, `## Forecast` → produced `.xlsx` has 3 sheets named "Revenue", "Expenses", "Forecast" with the tabular data.
- User asks an Agent: `"Generate a PPT summarizing yesterday's open PRs"` → Agent invokes `convert_to_document(markdown, 'pptx')` as a tool call; the agent's response contains a `.pptx` attachment chip (clickable to open, downloadable). User does not have to perform any additional convert step.
- Same user with a model that doesn't support tool calls falls back to the manual "Export → PPT" path on the markdown response; behavior is consistent.
- User exports a Note as PPT → same `loading` toast + success flow as for chat messages; same library path.
- Markdown with no detectable structure (single paragraph, no headings) when exported as PPT → single slide with the paragraph as body content (not a failure).
- Malformed markdown table (mismatched column count) exported as Excel → typed error toast `Failed to convert table — column counts don't match` with `View extracted preview` action; user clicks → modal shows what was parsed so they can spot the problem.
- DOCX export path is unchanged byte-for-byte from pre-feature behavior for the same markdown input.
- User exports a 30-page markdown to PDF → loading toast shows progress; no UI freeze; result file opens.

## Related

- #15279 (open, v2.2.0 — Pin agent-generated HTML apps to Launchpad; complementary, both productize Agent outputs but #15279 keeps the HTML form while this issue converts to document formats)
- #15398 (open, v2.4.0 — Launchpad surface for features and Agent artifacts; this issue's converted files can pin to that surface)
- #15029 (open, v2.1.0 — Built-In Skill Marketplace; the `convert_to_document` Agent tool can be packaged and shipped as a featured Skill)
- #15651 (related — Apply Error Classification to Toasts; conversion failures use the typed error path)
- #15653 (related — Complete Toast Coverage; conversion progress uses loading→success pattern)

title: [Feature]: Structured Agent Goals — Outcome-Driven Sessions with Progress Tracking and Completion Criteria
body:
## Background

Cherry Studio's Agent today is purely reactive: the user types, the Agent responds, repeat until the user stops or `max_turns` hits (default 100). There's no concept of "what are we trying to achieve in this session" — the `AgentEntity` schema has only `instructions` (system prompt) and `description` (free-form text); the `AgentSessionEntity` has no goal, no completion criterion, no progress field. The SDK's `plan` permission mode is exposed in the UI but treated only as a read-only-tool constraint, not as a planning workflow trigger — Cherry never asks the user "what's your goal?" the way Claude Code's Plan Mode, Cursor's Agent, or Cline's tasks do. The practical consequence: users open an Agent session, start describing a task in pieces, and the Agent has no anchor for "are we done yet?" — it just keeps responding turn-by-turn, often drifting, often re-asking for context the user already supplied, often producing output that doesn't ladder up to the original ask because the original ask was never named. Scheduled tasks have the same gap: they fire a plain `prompt` string with no notion of "succeeded" / "this run did the thing". Adding a structured `goal` concept turns Agent sessions from open-ended chats into outcome-driven workflows the user can actually see making progress.

## Goal

An Agent session can carry an explicit, user-set Goal that the Agent treats as the anchor for every turn — visibly tracked in the UI, referenced in the system prompt, evaluated for progress at the end of each turn, and explicitly marked done (by user confirmation or agent self-declaration with confirmation) so the user knows exactly when the work is finished.

## Spec

- A new optional `goal: string` field is added to `AgentSessionEntity` (per-session, not per-agent — different sessions of the same agent can have different goals).
- When a user starts a new Agent session, an inline goal-input banner appears above the conversation with the placeholder `"What are you trying to achieve in this session?"`. The user can fill it in, skip it, or set it later via the `/goal` slash command (registered alongside `/clear` per #15323).
- When a goal is set, every turn's system prompt includes a structured `Current goal: <goal text>` section. The Agent is instructed to (a) keep responses aligned with the goal, (b) at the end of each tool-use sequence, briefly note whether progress was made toward the goal.
- The session UI surfaces a persistent **Goal banner** at the top of the conversation — editable inline, with a small `Done` button to mark complete.
- The Agent can self-declare completion ("I believe the goal has been achieved — confirm?") which surfaces as an in-chat confirmation; user confirms or rejects.
- On goal completion (whether user-clicked or agent-self-declared + confirmed), the session is marked `goal_completed_at: timestamp`, a `success` toast (per #15653) confirms, and the goal banner switches to a `Goal achieved ✓` summary state.
- Optional sub-task decomposition: a user can ask the Agent `"break this goal into steps"` — the Agent produces a checklist; each item can be ticked off (or auto-ticked when the Agent reports completing it). This sub-task list is also stored on the session.
- Goal integrates with the existing `plan` permission mode: entering plan mode with a goal set causes the Agent to produce a read-only plan for achieving *that* specific goal rather than a generic "what would you like me to do" stance.
- Scheduled tasks (Cherry Claw) also gain an optional `goal` field separate from `prompt` — the `prompt` is the trigger text, the `goal` is what each fire is trying to accomplish; useful for distinguishing "remind me to drink water" (no goal, just message delivery) from "check yesterday's PRs and post a summary" (clear goal, agent should self-evaluate completion).
- Sessions without a goal behave exactly as today (no banner, no system-prompt injection, no completion tracking) — feature is opt-in per session.
- Goal text is editable any time during the session; the Agent's next turn picks up the new goal automatically.

## Verification

- User opens new Agent session → goal input banner appears with placeholder. User types `"Audit my Cherry Studio fork for security vulnerabilities"` → Goal banner persists at top of conversation showing the goal text.
- Session's first system prompt includes `Current goal: Audit my Cherry Studio fork for security vulnerabilities`. Agent's first response references the goal: "I'll start the audit. Let me first list the dependencies…"
- After 4 turns of Agent work, user types `/goal status` → Agent summarizes progress against the goal: "Audited 2 of 4 layers, found 3 candidate issues so far, remaining: API layer + storage layer".
- Agent finishes work and self-declares: `"I've completed the audit — 3 findings, here they are. Confirm goal completion?"` → user clicks `Confirm` → success toast `Goal achieved: Audit my Cherry Studio fork for security vulnerabilities`, banner switches to `Goal achieved ✓` summary.
- User edits the goal mid-session from `"Audit for security"` to `"Audit for security AND performance"` → next turn's system prompt reflects the new goal; Agent acknowledges and extends scope.
- User starts a new session and skips the goal input → no Goal banner appears; system prompt has no `Current goal` section; behavior is exactly as today.
- User in a goal-less session types `/goal Improve test coverage` → goal banner appears mid-session; next turn includes the new goal in system prompt.
- User asks `"Break this goal into steps"` → Agent produces a 4-item checklist; checklist is rendered in the goal panel; as Agent reports completing each item, the checkbox auto-ticks.
- User enters `plan` permission mode while a goal is set → Agent produces a read-only plan specifically for achieving that goal, not a generic "what should I do" plan.
- Scheduled Cherry Claw task with goal `"Triage yesterday's open PRs"` fires → after run, the task log records whether the goal was completed (agent self-evaluation, persisted on the scheduled run history).
- Existing Agent sessions on upgrade carry no goal — no behavior change, no banner.

## Related

- #15643 (related — Wire Up Missing Claude Agent SDK Capabilities; this issue's plan-mode-with-goal feature builds on #15643's permission-mode infrastructure)
- #15323 (open — `/clear` command in Agent session; this issue's `/goal` slash command registers via the same slash-command infrastructure)
- #15574 (related — Scheduled Task Message Perspective; this issue's scheduled-task-goal field is a natural extension)
- #15545 (related — "Create Skill" Entry Point; conceptually similar guided outcome pattern but scoped to Skills)
- #15028 (open, v2.0.0 — Onboarding lands users in Agent Chat with task cards; the task cards in #15028 are effectively pre-canned goals — this issue formalizes the concept for ongoing sessions)

title: [Feature]: Appshots — Screen Capture as Vision Input (User Button + Agent-Initiated Tool)
body:
## Background

Cherry Studio's screen-capture story today has three disjoint pieces and one missing one: (1) the bundled `@cherry/browser` MCP server can screenshot Playwright-managed browser tabs (`screenshot.ts`, `snapshot.ts`); (2) the renderer can capture Cherry's own UI via `html-to-image` (used for "Export message as image"); (3) the Selection Assistant can read system-wide selected text — but **none of these** can take a snapshot of the user's actual desktop, the foreground application, or a specific external window. The Electron primitive (`desktopCapturer.getSources()`) is unused; screen-recording permissions are not registered; there's no active-window detection. As a result, a user who wants the Agent to "look at this error on my screen" has to manually open a separate screenshot tool, save a file, drag it into chat, and explain what they're showing. Cursor's `@app`, Claude Desktop's screenshot button, and Anthropic's Computer Use all bridge this gap natively — Cherry's Agent is blind to the user's actual screen content even when it's a single API call away.

## Goal

Both the user (via a button in the chat composer) and an Agent (via a tool call) can capture the user's active window, full screen, or a specific application, and send the image directly as vision input to the model — with clear permission flow, visible capture indicator, and per-capture user control over what was actually grabbed.

## Spec

- A new **Screenshot button** in the chat composer (alongside the existing attachment button). Clicking opens a small source picker: `Full screen` / `Active window` / `Choose application` / `Choose region`.
- Behind the picker, Cherry uses Electron's `desktopCapturer.getSources({ types: ['screen', 'window'] })` to enumerate options and the appropriate platform-specific API to render the user's choice as a PNG.
- First use on each platform triggers OS-level screen-recording permission (macOS: System Settings > Privacy & Security > Screen Recording; Windows / Linux: equivalent). Cherry surfaces an in-app primer with rationale *before* the OS prompt fires; if the user denies, an in-app message with a one-click deep-link to the system settings appears.
- When a capture is in progress, a brief visible indicator (a 200ms screen flash + a subtle camera-shutter sound, like macOS's native screenshot) confirms the capture happened — no silent invisible captures.
- The captured image attaches to the user's current message as a normal image attachment (uses the same image pipeline as drag-drop / paste image), so existing send / vision-routing / preprocessing-for-non-vision-models (#15656) work unchanged.
- A new **Agent tool** `take_screenshot(target: 'active_window' | 'full_screen' | 'app:<bundle_id>' | 'region')` is registered. Agents can call it; the call requires per-call user approval by default (visible in chat as `Agent wants to take a screenshot of <target> — Allow?`), with an opt-in "Always allow for this agent" toggle that respects existing permission modes from #15643.
- Each agent screenshot tool call shows the captured image inline in the conversation as an agent observation, with a clear `📷 Captured from <target> at <timestamp>` caption. The image is visible to both the user and the model.
- Multi-monitor: when the user has multiple displays, the source picker shows each display with a preview thumbnail; the agent tool when used with `full_screen` defaults to the primary display unless the agent specifies a `display_index`.
- Active window detection uses the OS-native API per platform (macOS `NSWorkspace.frontmostApplication`, Windows `GetForegroundWindow`, Linux X11 `_NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW`). When no active window can be determined, the tool falls back to full-screen capture with a clear note in the response.
- All captured images are persisted only in the user's local conversation history — never sent to any Cherry-controlled telemetry / analytics. The image goes only to the model the user has explicitly selected.
- If the active model is not vision-capable, the image is preprocessed via #15656's existing OCR path before send, so even text-only models can benefit from the capture.

## Verification

- User clicks the new screenshot button in the chat composer → source picker shows `Full screen / Active window / Choose application / Choose region`. User picks `Active window` → 200ms flash + shutter sound → captured image appears as an attachment chip in the composer. User adds "what does this error mean?" and sends; GPT-5 (vision-capable) answers from the screenshot.
- First-ever use on macOS: in-app primer "Cherry needs Screen Recording permission to capture your screen" with `Continue` button → OS permission prompt → user grants → capture proceeds. User denies → in-app message with `Open System Settings > Privacy & Security > Screen Recording` deep link.
- User picks `Choose application` → list of running apps with icons (from `desktopCapturer.getSources()` window enumeration). User picks `Chrome` → Cherry captures only Chrome's window (not the rest of the desktop).
- Multi-display setup: source picker shows both displays as thumbnails labeled `Display 1 (primary)` and `Display 2 (1920×1080)`. User picks Display 2 → that display captured, not Display 1.
- Agent (with screenshot tool allowed) needs to see something to help: `Agent: "I'd like to take a screenshot of your active window to see the error — allow?"` → user clicks `Allow` → agent runs `take_screenshot('active_window')` → image appears inline in the conversation as agent observation with `📷 Captured from active window at <time>` caption.
- Same user with permission set to `dontAsk` (per #15643): agent's screenshot tool call is denied without prompt; in-chat note explains why.
- User with `auto` permission mode (per #15643): the model classifier decides per call — a tool call to `take_screenshot('full_screen')` triggers a prompt; `take_screenshot('active_window')` may pass silently if the user has previously approved similar calls.
- User on a text-only model takes a screenshot: per #15656 the image is preprocessed via OCR; the model receives text content and can answer.
- No telemetry: an inspector of network traffic during a screenshot send sees only the request to the user-selected model's API; no Cherry-controlled endpoint receives any image data.
- Existing chat / Agent flows that don't use screen capture are unchanged — no permission prompts, no behavior shifts.

## Related

- #15578 (related — Realtime Conversation Mode; complementary — #15578 covers continuous screen *stream* during voice/video, this issue covers discrete one-shot *snapshots* triggered by user button or agent tool. They share OS permission infrastructure but differ in capture cadence and use case)
- #15643 (related — Wire Up Missing Claude Agent SDK Capabilities; this issue's `take_screenshot` agent tool respects the permission modes added by #15643, especially `auto` for model-classified approval)
- #15656 (related — Preprocess Multimodal for Non-Vision Models; this issue's captured images route through #15656's OCR path when the active model is text-only)
- #15651 (related — Apply Error Classification to Toasts; permission-denied case surfaces as a typed error toast with `Open System Settings` inline action)

title: [Feature]: Support Anthropic Computer Use — OS-Level Mouse/Keyboard Automation Tool for Vision-Capable Agents
body:
## Background

Anthropic shipped Computer Use in October 2024 alongside Claude 3.5 Sonnet — a tool family (`computer`, `bash`, `text_editor`) where the model takes screenshots, emits mouse/keyboard actions, observes the result, and loops until task complete. Cherry Studio's situation today is split: the underlying SDK (`@anthropic-ai/sdk@0.81`, `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk@0.3.145`) **both ship Computer Use beta types natively**; the Anthropic provider's beta header builder (`src/main/ai/runtime/aiSdk/params/features/anthropicHeaders.ts:28-37`) already conditionally adds beta flags (`interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14`, `web-search-2025-03-05`); the model capability metadata in `packages/provider-registry/data/models.json` **already declares `computer-use`** on Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 4, 4.5, and Haiku 4.5. The agent runtime's tool-execution loop (`Agent.ts:134`, `loop/internal.ts:37-84`) is tool-agnostic and can host the new tool with minimal change. What's missing is the actual wiring: no `computer-use-2024-10-22` in the beta header set, no `computer` tool definition or handler, no OS automation library (no `robotjs`, no `@nut-tree-fork/nut-js`), no screenshot-after-action harness, no consumption of the `computer-use` capability flag to gate availability. Cherry Claw's prompt explicitly tells the agent "you do not have screenshot tools" today. Closing the gap turns Cherry's Agent from a code-only operator into something that can actually drive the user's desktop the same way Anthropic's reference implementation and Claude.ai's Computer Use demo do.

## Goal

Cherry Studio's Agent, when running on a Claude model that supports Computer Use, can autonomously take screenshots, click, type, scroll, and key-press on the user's desktop — looping until task completion — with explicit per-action user approval by default, full permission-mode integration (per #15643), and clear in-chat visibility of every action the Agent takes.

## Spec

- Cherry registers the **`computer` tool** (Anthropic Computer Use 2024-10-22 spec) when the active model's `computer-use` capability flag is true. The tool exposes the standard sub-actions: `screenshot`, `mouse_move`, `left_click`, `right_click`, `middle_click`, `double_click`, `left_click_drag`, `type`, `key`, `cursor_position`, `scroll`.
- The Anthropic provider's beta header builder is extended to include `computer-use-2024-10-22` when the active model supports it. Beta flags accumulate (multi-beta header), not replace.
- OS automation is provided by `@nut-tree-fork/nut-js` (cross-platform Node-native, MIT, maintained fork of nut-tree). The library is loaded only when the `computer` tool is enabled on an agent, to keep startup overhead off other code paths.
- Screenshot side is **shared with #15661** (Appshots): the same `ScreenCaptureService` + `screen:captureSource` IPC handles the model-initiated screenshots, so we don't have two parallel capture implementations.
- **Per-action approval is the default**: every `computer` tool call surfaces an inline approval in the chat with the action description (e.g. `Click at (450, 320) in the active window?`). The user clicks `Approve` / `Deny` / `Approve all in this session`. This is gated by #15643's permission modes:
  - `default`: approve per call
  - `acceptEdits`: still approve per call (mouse/keyboard isn't "an edit", it's a real-world action)
  - `bypassPermissions`: silent allow (use with caution; OS-level actions)
  - `plan`: tool not invocable (read-only constraint)
  - `dontAsk`: deny silently
  - `auto`: model-classifier per call — Cherry's classifier wraps the Anthropic model's risk assessment and prompts for high-risk actions (e.g. clicking inside browser address bar, typing into a terminal, dragging to delete)
- A **session-wide kill switch** (red stop button) is always visible when Computer Use is active — one click halts the agent's tool loop immediately, no matter where it is in the action sequence.
- Every action the Agent takes is logged in the conversation as a distinct event with a thumbnail of the screen state at that moment: `Clicked at (450, 320)` + small screenshot. The user can scroll back to see exactly what happened at each step.
- When the active model does **not** support Computer Use, the tool is not registered for that agent and the relevant menu items are hidden — no degraded UX.
- On first-ever use, Cherry surfaces a strong primer modal explaining what Computer Use does, the OS permissions it needs (screen recording + accessibility on macOS, etc.), and a "I understand" confirmation before enabling.
- Cherry Claw's prompt is updated to reflect the new capability when running on a Computer Use-capable model (today it explicitly disclaims screenshot tools).
- Sandbox option (per #15643): if the agent has `sandbox: enabled` and uses `computer`, Computer Use is silently disabled and the agent is told "computer tool unavailable in sandbox" — preventing the agent from breaking out of the sandbox via desktop actions.

## Verification

- User selects Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Computer Use-capable model), opens an Agent session, asks `"Open the Settings app and turn on Dark Mode"` → Agent's response shows a `screenshot` action requesting approval; user clicks `Approve` → screenshot taken → agent thinks → emits `mouse_move + left_click` approval request → user approves → eventually Dark Mode is on. Each step shown inline.
- User selects GPT-4 (no `computer-use` capability) and the same agent → the `computer` tool is not in the available tools list; agent says it doesn't have screen control.
- User with `bypassPermissions` mode runs the same task → no per-action prompts; agent autonomously completes; every action still logged with screen thumbnails in the conversation.
- User clicks the persistent red kill-switch mid-task → agent's next tool call is rejected; agent surfaces "Halted by user — current state: <last screenshot>"; conversation can continue normally.
- User on first-ever Computer Use enable → primer modal explains capability + permission requirements + risks → user confirms → tool becomes available for that agent.
- User has not granted macOS Accessibility permission → primer modal shows `Open System Settings > Privacy & Security > Accessibility` deep link; first tool use fails with a typed error toast (per #15651) and the same deep link.
- Sandbox-enabled agent with Computer Use available → tool is silently unregistered; agent's reasoning says "computer unavailable in sandbox"; bash and other tools continue working.
- Multi-monitor user: agent's first `screenshot` action defaults to primary display; agent can request specific display via `screenshot(display=1)`; user approval shows which display.
- `auto` permission mode + low-risk action like `mouse_move` → silent allow; `auto` + high-risk action like `type "rm -rf ~/"` in a Terminal window → forced approval with the model's risk reasoning shown.
- Agent attempts Computer Use on a model whose `computer-use` capability flag is falsely declared but the model doesn't actually support it → first tool call returns a typed error from the SDK; Cherry surfaces a `Model declared computer-use support but rejected the call` toast and disables the tool for the session.
- On upgrade, existing agents without `computer` in their `allowedTools` are unchanged; Computer Use is opt-in per agent.

## Related

- #15643 (related — Wire Up Missing Claude Agent SDK Capabilities; this issue's permission gating and sandbox interaction depend on #15643's `auto` / `dontAsk` modes and `sandbox` option)
- #15661 (related — Appshots; this issue **shares** the `ScreenCaptureService` and screen-recording permission flow with #15661 — both must use the same infra, not duplicate)
- #15656 (related — Preprocess Multimodal for Non-Vision Models; not directly used here since Computer Use requires vision-capable models by definition, but the OCR fallback could enhance Computer Use observation summaries)
- #15660 (related — Structured Agent Goals; Computer Use tasks naturally fit goal-driven sessions where progress = visible screen changes)
- #15651 (related — Apply Error Classification to Toasts; this issue's permission/capability errors use the typed error path)
- #11620 (open — older wishlist issue mentioning Computer Use; this issue is the focused implementation that supersedes #11620's Computer Use bullet)

title: [Feature]: Unified @ and / Command System — Codex-Style Discoverable Mentions and Slash Commands Across All Surfaces
body:
## Background

Cherry Studio's composer-input ecosystem for "quick references and quick actions" is fragmented across three asymmetric pieces today: (1) The `/` symbol only works as a **button-spawned menu** (not a text trigger) — typing `/` in the input does nothing, but clicking the slash-commands tool button opens a small menu of 5 commands (`/clear`, `/compact`, `/context`, `/cost`, `/todos`) that exist **only for Claude Code agents**; (2) Mention-style references use **different trigger symbols** for different things — `#` for knowledge bases, `?` for web search, file attachment is a separate button entirely, model selection is yet another button, mentioned models are tracked as `mentionedModels: Model[]` but populated via popover not text input; (3) The `@` symbol — the universal "mention this thing" convention from Slack, Cursor, Codex, Claude Code — is **completely unused** in Cherry's composer. Users who want to invoke a skill, switch agent mid-conversation, attach a folder, or reference a specific KB entry have no consistent muscle-memory shortcut — every action requires finding a different button. Codex's pattern (and Cursor's, and Claude Code's) is dead simple: type `/` for commands, type `@` for entities (files / agents / skills / KBs / models). Cherry's current state, where `/` is button-only and `@` is unused, is the bottom of the discoverability spectrum. Unifying these into one input-triggered system with a single registry — that any built-in feature or user-installed Skill can extend — closes the gap and gives users one shortcut to remember.

## Goal

Typing `/` in any composer input opens a command palette listing all commands available in the current context (built-in + skill-provided + agent-specific); typing `@` opens an entity palette listing files, folders, agents, skills, knowledge bases, models, and prompts — both with fuzzy search, keyboard navigation, and one-button activation, working identically across chat, agent, side chat, and temporary chat surfaces.

## Spec

- **`/` becomes a real text trigger** in the composer: typing `/` opens an inline command palette that filters as the user types. Existing button-spawned slash menu is removed in favor of this single input-triggered flow.
- **`@` becomes the universal entity trigger**: typing `@` opens an inline entity palette covering: `@file`, `@folder`, `@url`, `@agent`, `@skill`, `@kb`, `@model`, `@prompt`. Each entity type can be filtered by typing further (e.g. `@code` filters to entities containing "code" across all types).
- **The existing `#` (KB) and `?` (web search) triggers are migrated**: `#kb-name` becomes `@kb:kb-name`, `?query` becomes a search command surfaced via `/search`. Old triggers continue working for a transition period (one release cycle) with an inline hint suggesting the new syntax.
- **Unified command registry** — a single `CommandRegistry` exposes:
  - `registerCommand({ name, description, surface, handler })` — Cherry's built-in commands and Skills can both register; surface filter (chat / agent / skill-creator / all) controls visibility.
  - The 5 existing Claude Code commands move into this registry with `surface: 'agent'`.
  - Skills can declare commands in their `SKILL.md` frontmatter (`commands: ['/skill-name', '/skill-name --quick']`) so user-installed Skills automatically populate the palette.
- **Unified entity registry** — same pattern for `@`: `registerEntityProvider({ type, search, render })` where each type (file / agent / skill / KB / model / prompt) has a provider that returns matching entities given a query string. New entity types added by Skills or future features hook in without touching the palette UI.
- **Cross-surface consistency**: the same `/` and `@` palettes work identically in chat, agent, side chat (per #15452 if implemented), and temporary chat (per #15576). Surface-specific commands are visibly grouped (e.g. `/clear` only shown in agent surface).
- **Agent switching mid-chat**: typing `@agent:reviewer` lets the next message be routed to a different agent in the same conversation — supporting power workflows like "let CodeReviewer look at this snippet, then back to main agent". The receiving agent gets the relevant context excerpt automatically.
- **Skill invocation via `/`**: typing `/skill-name` invokes a Skill explicitly (today Skills only trigger via description matching). Explicit invocation is faster and more discoverable for power users.
- **Keyboard support**: `/` and `@` open the palette; `↑↓` navigate; `Enter` accepts; `Esc` dismisses; `Tab` accepts and stays open for chained selection; type-to-filter is always on.
- **Discoverability**: when the user has no `/` or `@` activity, an unobtrusive first-time hint appears in the composer: `Tip: type / for commands, @ for files & agents`. Dismissable.

## Verification

- User types `/` in chat composer → palette opens listing available commands (filtered by current surface). Typing `co` filters to `/compact`, `/context`, `/cost`. Enter selects.
- User types `@` → palette shows entity types as section headers (`Files`, `Agents`, `Skills`, `Knowledge Bases`, `Models`, `Prompts`). Typing `read` filters across all types to matching entities (e.g. `README.md` under Files, `CodeReader` under Agents).
- User types `@agent:CodeReviewer` in mid-conversation with Cherry Assistant → next message routed to CodeReviewer agent; the response appears inline with `From CodeReviewer:` label; main agent context is preserved.
- User installs a Skill whose `SKILL.md` declares `commands: ['/summarize-pr']` → after install, typing `/sum` in chat surfaces `/summarize-pr` in the palette; selecting it invokes the Skill directly.
- User types `#docs-kb` (legacy syntax) → palette still shows the KB picker but with an inline hint `Tip: use @kb:docs-kb in future`; selection works as today.
- User in temporary chat (per #15576) types `/` → palette opens with the same commands as a regular chat; surface filter respects the ephemeral context (e.g. `/clear` works, `/cost` works).
- User in agent surface types `/` → palette includes both the 5 Claude Code commands AND any user-skill-provided commands AND `@`-style entity commands like `/agent:switch-to`.
- Power-user keyboard flow: `@`, type `read`, `↓` to navigate, `Enter` accepts → file mention inserted; user continues typing → `@`, type `code`, `Tab` to accept and stay open, picks an agent → both mentions in the same message.
- First-time user in a fresh install sees the discoverability tip `Tip: type / for commands, @ for files & agents` once per surface; dismisses; never sees it again on that surface.
- On upgrade, existing button-spawned slash menu and current `#` / `?` triggers continue to work for one release cycle; deprecation hint surfaces inline on use; after the cycle, only the new unified system is supported.
- Skill that registers a command with `surface: 'chat-only'` does not appear when the user is in an agent surface — surface filtering verified.

## Related

- #15323 (open — `/clear` command in Agent session; this issue's unified `/` system includes `/clear` and all other slash commands; #15323 is partially superseded — its mechanism is absorbed)
- #15452 (open — `/btw` side question + queue injection; the `/btw` command registers via this issue's command registry once both land)
- #15545 (related — "Create Skill" Entry Point; this issue's `/` palette includes a `/new-skill` command that triggers the Skill Creator entry flow)
- #15576 (related — Temporary Chat; this issue's `/` and `@` work identically in temporary chats per the "cross-surface consistency" spec)
- #15660 (related — Structured Agent Goals; this issue's `/goal set` / `/goal status` / `/goal done` slash commands register through the unified system)
- #15643 (related — SDK Capabilities; this issue's `/effort` / `/thinking` slash commands surface the controls #15643 exposes)
- #10741 (closed historical — Discoverable Slash Command Platform for Agent Workflows; closed without implementation; this issue is the focused redo with broader scope including `@` mentions)

title: [Feature]: In-Message Annotations on Agent HTML Artifacts
body:
## Background

When an Agent produces an HTML report or dashboard in a session, the only way for a user to refine it today is to type free-form feedback into the next message ("the chart on the right uses the wrong color, and the second card is too wide"). The Agent has to guess which chart, which card. Users either give up or re-prompt from scratch and lose a v1 they were 90% happy with. HTML artifacts are especially affected because the things users want to fix are often discrete visual elements (a chart bar, a card, an image), not just text.

This is the HTML counterpart of the Markdown artifact annotation framework defined in #15666; it reuses that framework and adds element-level anchoring. (Split out from the combined #15607.)

## Goal

In the current session, users can annotate specific text regions and discrete visual elements of the most recent HTML artifact in an Agent reply, then send those annotations to the Agent as one precisely-anchored revision request that produces a new reply.

## Spec

- HTML artifacts in an Agent message support two annotation kinds: text-selection annotations (highlight a span of rendered text) and element-pointer annotations (click a discrete visual element — e.g. a chart bar, a card, an image — to pin a comment to that element).
- The feature reuses the shared annotation framework from #15666: each annotation is one comment on one anchor; the artifact view shows all pending annotations as highlights/markers with a side panel listing them; submission has a default batch mode ("Send to Agent") plus a per-annotation "Send now".
- The dispatched message describes each element-pointer annotation by a stable descriptor (e.g. tag + text/index path) so the Agent can unambiguously locate the element in the source, including HTML that fetches live data from an external API.
- Sending posts a structured user message carrying each annotation (anchor description + anchored excerpt/element + user comment); pending annotations are cleared from the artifact on send.
- The Agent's response is a normal next message; if it contains a new HTML artifact, that artifact becomes annotatable in the same way. Prior artifacts in scrollback are read-only — no new annotations can be added to a superseded artifact.
- Annotations are session-local and ephemeral: they live only until sent or discarded, are not persisted across app restarts, and are not visible to anyone else.

## Verification

- In an Agent reply containing an HTML dashboard, click a specific chart bar, add comment "this bar should use brand primary, not gray" → the annotation marker stays pinned to that bar while the user scrolls within the artifact view or resizes the side panel.
- On the same HTML artifact, add one text-selection annotation on a heading and two element-pointer annotations on two cards, click "Send to Agent" once → all three are bundled into a single user message; the Agent's resulting reply addresses all three.
- On a single annotation, click "Send now" → only that annotation is dispatched; other pending annotations remain visible for later sending.
- An HTML artifact that fetches live data from an external API still accepts element-pointer annotations; the dispatched message describes the element by a stable descriptor so the Agent can identify it unambiguously in source.
- After a successful send, the just-sent annotations are cleared from the artifact view (markers gone, side panel empty for that batch).
- Scroll up to a prior (now superseded) HTML artifact → it is read-only: selecting text or clicking elements does not offer the annotation affordance.
- Attempt "Send to Agent" with zero pending annotations → the action is disabled with a tooltip explaining why; saving a comment with empty text is likewise disabled until text is entered.
- Discard a pending annotation → its marker disappears from the artifact and the side panel; no message is sent.
- Close and reopen the app while annotations are pending → the pending annotations are gone (ephemeral); the underlying Agent reply is unchanged.

## Related

#15666 #15279 #15398

title: [Feature]: In-Message Annotations on Agent Markdown Artifacts
body:
## Background

When an Agent produces a long Markdown document in a session, the only way for a user to refine it today is to type free-form feedback into the next message ("the third paragraph is wrong, and the second bullet should be removed"). The Agent has to guess which paragraph, which bullet. Users either give up, or re-prompt from scratch and lose a v1 they were 90% happy with.

This issue defines the base annotation framework (anchoring, side panel, batch dispatch, ephemerality); #15665 extends the same framework to HTML artifacts with element-level anchoring. (Split out from the combined #15607.)

## Goal

In the current session, users can annotate specific text spans of the most recent Markdown artifact in an Agent reply, then send those annotations to the Agent as one precisely-anchored revision request that produces a new reply.

## Spec

- Markdown artifacts in an Agent message support text-selection annotations: the user highlights a span of rendered text, opens a comment, and the comment is anchored to that span.
- Each annotation is a single comment attached to one anchor; the artifact view shows all pending annotations as highlights/markers with a side panel listing them.
- Submission is user-driven with two modes: a default batch mode (multiple annotations accumulate; the user clicks "Send to Agent" to dispatch the whole batch as one revision request) and a per-annotation "Send now" action that immediately dispatches just that annotation.
- Sending a batch posts a structured user message to the session carrying each annotation as (anchor description + anchored excerpt + user comment); pending annotations are cleared from the artifact on send.
- The Agent's response is a normal next message; if it contains a new Markdown artifact, that new artifact becomes annotatable in the same way. Prior artifacts in scrollback are read-only — no new annotations can be added to a superseded artifact.
- Annotations are session-local and ephemeral: they live only until sent or discarded, are not persisted across app restarts, and are not visible to anyone else.

## Verification

- In an Agent reply containing a Markdown weekly report, highlight the phrase "Q3 revenue grew 12%", add comment "should be 15%", click "Send to Agent" → a new user message appears in the session carrying the annotation; the Agent's next reply produces a corrected report.
- On the same Markdown artifact, add three annotations on three different paragraphs, click "Send to Agent" once → all three are bundled into a single user message; the Agent's resulting reply addresses all three.
- On a single annotation, click "Send now" → only that annotation is dispatched; any other pending annotations remain visible on the artifact for later sending.
- After a successful send, the just-sent annotations are cleared from the artifact view (markers gone, side panel empty for that batch).
- Scroll up to a prior Agent reply (now superseded): the older artifact is read-only — selecting text does not offer the annotation affordance.
- Attempt to click "Send to Agent" with zero pending annotations → the action is disabled with a tooltip explaining why; attempting to save a comment with empty text is likewise disabled until text is entered.
- Discard a pending annotation → the marker disappears from the artifact and from the side panel; no message is sent.
- Close and reopen the app while annotations are pending → the pending annotations are gone (ephemeral, as specified); the underlying Agent reply is unchanged.

## Related

title: [Feature]: One-Click Error Reporting from Error Toasts and Dialogs
body:
## Background

When users hit an error, Cherry Studio shows a toast or dialog with a message, but there's no easy way to send that error back to the team. Diagnosing relies on users manually copying logs or filing a GitHub issue with incomplete context — so most just dismiss the error. The team has no way to monitor how often real-world errors occur or to get the context needed to locate and fix them.

## Goal

From an error toast or dialog, the user can click "Report" to send that error's diagnostic details to Cherry's server in one action and get back a reference ID, so the team can monitor and locate issues.

## Spec

- Error toasts and error dialogs carry a "Report" / feedback action.
- Clicking it submits the error's diagnostic context (error type/message, stack, app version, OS/platform, the failing module/operation, and recent relevant logs) to Cherry's server in one action — no manual copying.
- Reporting is **explicitly user-initiated per occurrence**; nothing is uploaded automatically. The user can preview exactly what will be sent before it's sent.
- Credentials and conversation content are never included: API keys, tokens, and message text are redacted from the payload.
- On success the user gets a confirmation with a reference / trace ID they can quote (e.g. in a GitHub issue or to support); a failed submit is surfaced with a retry/copy option, never silent.
- Submitted reports are aggregatable server-side by error signature, so the team can monitor frequency and triage.

## Verification

- Trigger an error (e.g. invalid API key) → the toast shows a "Report" action; click it → one submit happens, then a confirmation toast shows a reference ID.
- Use the preview before sending → user sees error type, stack, version, OS, module, but does NOT see their API key or message text.
- Click "Report" while offline → a clear "couldn't send report" message with retry/copy, not a silent no-op.
- An error shown as a modal dialog (not just a toast) → offers the same "Report" action.
- Dismiss/ignore the error toast → nothing is uploaded.
- The same error reported by multiple users → server can group them by error signature for frequency monitoring.

## Related

title: [Feature]: User-Level Memory Shared Across All Agents (Implementation of #14738)
body:
## Background

Issue #14738 was filed in April 2026 with the title "Auto-Memory in Agent Mode (User-Level)" and a detailed Spec describing a **two-tier memory architecture**: (1) user-level memory shared across all of a user's agents — for durable facts like environment quirks, recurring fixes, long-lived preferences — and (2) per-agent workspace memory for project-specific context that should not leak across agents. The Spec was clear: *"User-level memory is shared across all of the user's agents — what one agent writes is visible to all others. Each agent's per-agent (workspace) memory continues to exist for context that should not leak across agents."* The issue was closed in May 2026 — but with no associated PR (`closedByPullRequestsReferences: []`), no commit references in git history, and grep across the renderer + main returns zero matches for `userMemory`, `USER_MEMORY`, `cross_agent`, or `shared.memory`. Verification of the actual implementation confirms only the per-agent workspace tier exists today: `workspaceMemory.ts:158-168`'s `getWorkspacePath()` resolves to `{workspace}/memory/`, which is per-agent; Cherry Claw's prompt literally tells the agent `"persistent memory in this agent's workspace"`. So #14738's headline feature — the user-level tier — was never implemented; the issue was closed administratively. This issue is the focused implementation: build the user-level memory layer that #14738 promised, alongside (not replacing) the existing per-agent tier.

## Goal

Cherry agents have access to two memory tiers — a new user-level tier shared across all of a user's agents for durable user-wide facts, and the existing per-agent workspace tier for context that should not leak — with the agent itself deciding which tier to write to based on a durability heuristic, and a user-visible UI showing both tiers separately so the user can audit and edit each independently.

## Spec

- A new user-level memory location is established at a per-user, agent-agnostic path: `application.getPath('user.memory', 'USER_FACT.md')` (resolved to e.g. `~/.config/CherryStudio/memory/USER_FACT.md` on Linux, equivalent on macOS / Windows). Goes through the existing path registry, not ad-hoc.
- A sibling `USER_JOURNAL.jsonl` lives alongside for timestamped user-level events.
- The existing `mcp__agent-memory__memory` tool gains a `scope: 'agent' | 'user'` parameter (default `'agent'` to preserve current behavior). `scope: 'user'` reads/writes the user-level tier; `scope: 'agent'` keeps today's per-agent behavior unchanged.
- The agent system prompt is updated to instruct: "write user-level facts (recurring user preferences, environment, long-lived identity facts) with `scope: 'user'`; write project-specific facts (this codebase uses X, this client wants Y) with `scope: 'agent'`. When unsure, default to `scope: 'agent'` — user-level memory affects all your other agents."
- When an agent session starts, both `USER_FACT.md` (user-level) and `{workspace}/memory/FACT.md` (per-agent) are loaded into the system prompt, with clear section headers (`## User-Level Facts` and `## Agent Workspace Facts`) so the model knows which is which and which to write back to.
- Precedence on conflict: if a user-level fact and a per-agent fact contradict, both are surfaced to the model with a clear note (`Note: user-level says X, agent workspace says Y`). The model decides how to handle for the current task; neither layer silently overrides.
- A new Settings page (or section under existing Agent settings) exposes both memory tiers: user can view, edit, and delete entries in user-level memory; per-agent memory editing remains where it is today.
- Per-agent isolation is **explicitly preserved** — nothing changes about how `{workspace}/memory/FACT.md` works. Agent A and Agent B still cannot read each other's per-agent memory (this was the only thing that *was* implemented from #14738's Spec).
- On upgrade, existing per-agent FACT.md files are untouched. A new empty `USER_FACT.md` is created for each user; the agent begins to populate it on the next session as it identifies durable cross-agent facts.
- Cherry's built-in agents (Cherry Claw / Cherry Assistant / Skill Creator) all participate in user-level memory by default. User-created agents inherit the same default but can opt out per-agent (a setting field `userMemoryEnabled: boolean`, default true).
- The memory deduplication issue at #15411 (memory dedup ignores scope) becomes more critical with two tiers — coordinate fix: dedup must respect both `scope` AND the speaker scope from #15600's channel-user identity work, otherwise user A's user-level fact dedupes against user B's same-text fact.

## Verification

- User runs Agent A and tells it `"I work in TypeScript and prefer pnpm"`. Agent identifies this as a user-level durable fact and writes via `scope: 'user'` → `~/.config/CherryStudio/memory/USER_FACT.md` contains the entry.
- Same user opens Agent B (different agent, never used). Agent B's system prompt now contains `## User-Level Facts` section including the TypeScript + pnpm preference. User asks "recommend a build tool" → Agent B's answer reflects the known preferences without re-asking.
- User opens Agent A again and asks it to add a project-specific fact: `"This codebase uses Tailwind v4"`. Agent identifies this as project-scoped and writes via `scope: 'agent'` → `{Agent-A-workspace}/memory/FACT.md` contains the entry; `USER_FACT.md` does not change.
- User opens Agent B and asks about CSS conventions → Agent B's `## Agent Workspace Facts` section does NOT contain the Tailwind v4 fact (because that's Agent A's workspace). Agent B answers without assuming Tailwind v4. Per-agent isolation preserved.
- User opens Settings → Memory → user-level pane shows TypeScript + pnpm entries; can delete the pnpm entry inline; next Agent B session no longer references pnpm preference.
- Conflict test: User manually edits `USER_FACT.md` to say "I prefer npm" while Agent A's workspace still says "user prefers pnpm" → next session both facts surface in the system prompt with a `Note: user-level says npm, agent workspace says pnpm` note; agent asks user which to honor going forward.
- User creates a new agent with `userMemoryEnabled: false` → that agent's system prompt has no `## User-Level Facts` section; the agent operates in isolation.
- Cherry Claw's heartbeat fire respects user-level memory — it can read user-level facts when generating its heartbeat prompt.
- On upgrade, an existing user with populated per-agent workspaces sees no behavior change for per-agent memory; a new empty `USER_FACT.md` exists; the next agent run starts populating it autonomously as cross-agent facts are identified.
- `mcp__agent-memory__memory` tool calls with no `scope` parameter default to `scope: 'agent'` — full backward compatibility for any callers not aware of the new param.

## Related

- #14738 (closed historical, May 2026 — original Spec; this issue is its delayed implementation. The administrative closure without PR is documented in the Background above)
- #15411 (open — Memory deduplication ignores user and assistant scope; becomes more critical with two tiers; coordinate fix to respect both `scope` and the channel-user identity from #15600)
- #15600 (related — Multi-User Identity in External IM Channel Adapters; in channel scenarios, user-level memory must be scoped per channel-user to prevent the cross-user leak this session already filed)
- #15660 (related — Structured Agent Goals; goals are session-scoped, complementary to memory's user-scoped / agent-scoped tiers)
- #15643 (related — Wire Up Missing Claude Agent SDK Capabilities; this issue's memory tool extension is a small addition to the existing tool surface)

title: [Feature]: Inline-Rendered Generative UI Components in Chat
body:
## Background

When the AI produces a generative UI component (a chart, dashboard, or form) as HTML, Cherry Studio currently shows a collapsed artifact card in the message. The user must click "Preview" to open a separate popup before they can see the rendered result or reuse it. The rendered output is never visible inline, and quick actions are one click deep. Peer products like cowork render such generative UI directly in the conversation as a visual component that can be copied as an image or opened as HTML on the spot.

## Goal

Users see AI-generated UI components rendered visually and inline within the chat message, and can copy a component as an image or open it as HTML directly from that inline component.

## Spec

- When an AI reply contains a generative UI component (HTML for a chart, dashboard, or form), it renders inline as a visual preview within the message — not as a collapsed card that requires a click to view.
- The inline preview shows the final rendered appearance of the component; in-place interactivity is not required (visualization only).
- The inline component exposes a "copy as image" action that places a PNG snapshot of the rendered component on the clipboard.
- The inline component exposes an "open HTML" action that opens the full component in an expanded/external view.
- Streaming output renders progressively without breaking message layout, settling into the final rendered component once complete.

## Verification

- AI replies with a bar chart → the chart renders inline as a visual chart, with no "Preview" click required first.
- On an inline component, click "copy as image" → pasting into another app shows the rendered component as a PNG image, not the HTML source text.
- On an inline component, click "open HTML" → the full component opens in an expanded/external view.
- AI replies with a form layout (inputs + submit button) → it displays inline as a rendered visual, without needing to be interactive.
- A long component streamed token-by-token renders progressively and does not overflow or break the surrounding message layout.

## Related

#11424 #15638 #15607

title: [Feature]: Skill Suite — Bundle Related Skills with Shared Setup, Auth, and Composition
body:
## Background

Cherry Studio's Skill model today is strictly **atomic**: one install equals one skill, one `SKILL.md`, one directory under `{dataPath}/Skills/{folderName}/`. The metadata schema (`markdownParser.ts:297-410`) supports only `name / description / version / author / tools / tags` — there is no `dependencies`, `suite`, `group`, `bundle`, or any other grouping primitive. `SkillService.install()` takes a single identifier and unpacks a single directory; no multi-skill atomic install exists. Skills cannot share authentication, configuration, binary installation, or any other resource — each skill must reimplement setup independently. The closest precedent is the `cherry-assistant` built-in agent, whose `agent.json` lists 4 skills (`cherry-assistant-guide`, `faq-collector`, `issue-reporter`, `skills-manager`) — but these are independently installed and toggled, sharing nothing structurally. Meanwhile, the reference pattern this issue is modeled after — the Lark/Feishu unified CLI suite — provides **one install** that brings in 11 cohesive sub-skill domains (IM, docs, sheets, base, calendar, task, mail, wiki, video conference, contacts, events), all sharing one OAuth flow, one CLI binary, one shared auth/permission layer, plus workflow skills that compose across domains and a custom skill-maker for users to extend the suite. Cherry users authoring or installing collections of related skills (a "WeCom suite", a "Notion suite", an "AWS suite", a "Cherry Studio internal-tools suite") today have to maintain each sub-skill as a separate install, re-do auth setup for each, and have no way to ship a coherent workflow that composes across them. This issue introduces Skill Suite as a first-class entity that closes the gap.

## Goal

Skill authors and end users can install, version, configure, and uninstall a Skill Suite as a single unit; the suite atomically brings in its sub-skills, shares one setup/auth path across them, supports workflow sub-skills that compose other sub-skills, and surfaces in the Marketplace as a first-class kind alongside individual Skills.

## Spec

- A Skill Suite is declared by a top-level `suite.yaml` (or `SUITE.md` frontmatter, matching the existing skill pattern) at the suite directory root, with metadata: `name`, `description`, `version`, `allowed-tools`, `sub-skills: [...]`, `shared-setup` (optional path to a setup script), `depends-on` (optional list of other suites/skills), and `skill-maker` (optional reference to a custom-skill-maker sub-skill).
- Each sub-skill remains a regular `SKILL.md` directory under the suite root (e.g. `lark-unified/lark-im/SKILL.md`, `lark-unified/lark-doc/SKILL.md`). Sub-skills inherit suite-level `version` and `allowed-tools` unless they declare their own.
- **Atomic install**: installing a suite installs all listed sub-skills in one operation. The user sees one entry in the Skill library labeled `<suite-name> (suite)` with a sub-skills expandable section showing each domain; or each sub-skill listed with a `Part of: <suite-name>` badge — both views available, user preference toggle in Skills settings.
- **Atomic uninstall**: uninstalling a suite removes all its sub-skills together with a confirmation that lists exactly which sub-skills will go.
- **Per-sub-skill enable/disable**: although install is atomic, **each sub-skill can be individually enabled or disabled per agent** — users can install the lark-unified suite but disable `lark-mail` for a specific agent if that agent doesn't need email. This preserves today's per-agent skill toggling UX while adding the suite layer above it.
- **Shared setup**: when a suite is first invoked, the `shared-setup` script runs once for the whole suite (e.g. install `lark-cli` binary, run OAuth device flow, persist credentials). Subsequent invocations of any sub-skill reuse the shared setup state. The setup script's lifecycle (begin → poll → save) is exposed to the skill so it can show progress to the user via the toast / loading patterns from #15653.
- **Workflow sub-skills**: a sub-skill can declare `type: workflow` in its frontmatter, with `composes: [<sibling-sub-skill-names>]`. Workflow sub-skills can invoke composed siblings as documented tools rather than re-implementing each domain. (Example: `lark-workflow-meeting-summary` composes `lark-vc` + `lark-doc`.)
- **Skill-maker pattern**: a suite can ship a `skill-maker` sub-skill that lets users author custom sub-skills within the same suite (inheriting the shared setup/auth) — the maker writes new `SKILL.md` files into the suite's directory and they show up after registration.
- **Marketplace surface** (#15029 / #14876): the in-app Skill Marketplace shows Suites as a distinct kind alongside individual Skills; a suite card displays sub-skill count, version, and description; install button installs the whole suite.
- **Version updates**: a suite version bump cascades to all sub-skills atomically. Sub-skills cannot be individually version-pinned (avoids drift); for advanced users, the suite manifest supports `sub-skill-version-overrides` for explicit pinning.
- **Backward compat**: every existing individual Skill keeps working unchanged. Suites are an additive concept; the existing `SkillService.install()` single-skill path is preserved verbatim. A skill can opt in to being part of a suite later by being moved into a suite directory + re-registered.
- **`/` palette integration** (#15664): suite-level commands appear in the unified `/` palette grouped under the suite name; sub-skill commands appear under the same group.

## Verification

- User installs `lark-unified` suite via the Marketplace → one `loading` toast `Installing lark-unified (11 sub-skills)…` → on completion, 11 sub-skills (lark-im, lark-doc, lark-sheets, lark-base, lark-calendar, lark-task, lark-mail, lark-wiki, lark-vc, lark-contact, lark-event) appear in the Skill library with `Part of: lark-unified` badges.
- User invokes any lark sub-skill for the first time → suite's `shared-setup` runs once: installs `lark-cli`, opens OAuth device-flow URL in browser, polls until completion, saves credentials. A `loading` toast shows progress per setup phase.
- User invokes a second lark sub-skill (any) → shared setup state is reused; no second OAuth prompt.
- User in Agent A's settings disables `lark-mail` (per-agent toggle) → Agent A can still use `lark-im` / `lark-doc` / others, but `lark-mail` is unavailable. Agent B (separate) still has `lark-mail` enabled.
- User invokes `lark-workflow-meeting-summary` (a workflow sub-skill) → it transparently calls `lark-vc` + `lark-doc` as composed tools; result is a single aggregated meeting summary file.
- User uninstalls `lark-unified` suite → confirmation modal lists all 11 sub-skills that will be removed; on confirm, all 11 disappear in one operation; the per-agent enabled/disabled state for those sub-skills is wiped.
- User publishes their own suite `aws-toolkit` containing sub-skills `aws-s3 / aws-lambda / aws-ec2 / aws-iam` via CherryIN (#14876) → suite shows in Marketplace as a suite card with sub-skill count `4`; install brings all four.
- User uses the suite's `skill-maker` (if present) to write a custom `aws-cloudwatch` sub-skill → after the maker registers it, it appears under `aws-toolkit` with full inherited setup; no separate auth flow.
- User types `/lark` in the `/` palette (#15664) → palette shows all lark-* sub-skill commands grouped under `lark-unified`.
- Marketplace surface shows two kinds clearly distinguished: individual Skills and Suites. Filtering by kind works as expected.
- On upgrade, existing standalone Skills installed via the current single-skill path keep working — `SkillService.install()` single-skill behavior is byte-for-byte preserved.
- Suite manifest validation rejects: missing sub-skills directories, circular workflow `composes`, sub-skill name collisions across suites in the same library.

## Related

- #15545 (related — "Create Skill" Entry Point; the Suite's `skill-maker` pattern extends this issue's guided creation flow with suite-scoped authoring)
- #15029 (open, v2.1.0 — Built-In Skill Marketplace; this issue adds Suites as a first-class kind alongside individual Skills in the Marketplace surface)
- #14876 (open, v2.2.0 — CherryIN Integration / Save-as-Skill; this issue's suite publishing path goes through CherryIN with a new submission flow for suites)
- #15036 (open, v2.2.0 — Share Installed Skills via Cherry Mail; this issue's suite shareable as one unit instead of N peer shares)
- #15340 (open, v2.4.0 — Marketplace Connectors via OAuth/MCP; complementary — Connectors are external service auth, Suites are skill bundles; an MCP-form Connector could be a sub-skill within a Suite)
- #15643 (related — Wire Up Missing Claude Agent SDK Capabilities; suite `allowed-tools` inherits the same SDK permission model)
- #15653 (related — Complete Toast Coverage; suite install / shared-setup uses the loading→success toast pattern)
- #15664 (related — Unified @ and / Command System; suite commands and sub-skill commands surface in the unified palette grouped by suite)

## Reference implementation

The canonical example this issue is modeled on is the **Lark/Feishu unified CLI suite** (`lark-unified`), which ships as ONE skill that internally provides ~11 sub-skill domains (`lark-im`, `lark-doc`, `lark-sheets`, `lark-base`, `lark-calendar`, `lark-task`, `lark-mail`, `lark-wiki`, `lark-vc`, `lark-contact`, `lark-event`) plus workflow skills (`lark-workflow-meeting-summary`, `lark-workflow-standup-report`) plus a custom skill-maker (`lark-skill-maker`). All share one OAuth flow, one CLI binary (`lark-cli`), one shared auth/permission layer, and expose 200+ commands across 11 integrated business domains. This issue's spec is the Cherry-Studio-native equivalent of that pattern.

title: [Feature]: AI-Suggested Next Prompt as Inline Ghost Text in the Empty Composer
body:
## Background

When a user finishes reading an Assistant or Agent reply and the composer is empty, there is no continuation hint. The user has to think from a cold start — what to ask next, how to follow up, what's a natural next step — and many users either trail off mid-conversation or paste vague `"继续"` / `"more"` because crafting a precise follow-up is high friction. Cherry Studio already has the conversation context in hand (passed into the composer) and a configured fast model (today used only for topic auto-rename). Nothing surfaces a suggested next prompt to the user despite both ingredients being right there.

## Goal

When the chat composer is empty and focused, Cherry Studio shows a single AI-generated suggested next prompt as inline ghost text inside the input — the user can hit Tab to accept and edit, or just start typing to dismiss — using the same fast model already configured for topic auto-rename.

## Spec

- When the chat composer gains focus AND its text is empty AND the current conversation has at least one prior message, Cherry Studio generates a single suggested next prompt from the recent conversation context and displays it as italic gray ghost text inside the composer, with a `⇥ Tab to accept` hint at the right edge.
- The suggestion uses the same fast model the user has already configured under Topic Auto-Rename settings; if no fast model is configured, the feature silently degrades (no ghost text, no error, composer behaves exactly as today).
- `Tab` accepts: the ghost text is committed as editable text with the cursor at the end. Any other keystroke, clicking outside the composer, or `Esc` dismisses silently — no toast, no error log.
- At most one suggestion is generated per Assistant / Agent reply; after the next assistant message lands, the next time the user empties + focuses the composer the suggestion regenerates.
- The generation call is non-blocking: composer is fully usable while the suggestion is in flight; if the user starts typing before the suggestion arrives, the in-flight call is cancelled and no ghost text appears.
- Feature is opt-in via a toggle in Quick Model settings (alongside the Topic Auto-Rename toggle): `Suggested next prompt`, default **off**.

## Verification

- User just read an Assistant response about React hooks, clicks the empty composer → within ~1-2s, ghost text appears: `e.g. How does useCallback differ from useMemo in practice?` + `⇥ Tab to accept`. User hits Tab → text fills the input as editable; user appends ` with a code example` and sends.
- User focuses the empty composer and immediately starts typing → ghost text never appears (in-flight call cancelled).
- Conversation is in Chinese: ghost text appears in Chinese (e.g. `再举一个 useMemo 的实际例子？`), matching the conversation's language.
- User toggles `Suggested next prompt` off → composer no longer shows ghost text on focus; existing conversations behave as before.
- User opens a brand-new topic with zero messages → focuses composer → no ghost text; composer shows only its placeholder.
- User has not configured a topic-naming fast model → focuses composer in an existing conversation → no ghost text, no error toast, composer behaves exactly as today.

## Related

- #15307 (related — Topic Auto-Rename Toggle; this feature reuses #15307's existing fast-model preference)
- #15260 (related — Multiple Prompt Boxes; orthogonal — that's user-curated prompt sections, this is AI-suggested next prompts)
- #15570 (related — Guided Creation Flow for Assistants and Agents; similar guided-input UX pattern, scoped to entity creation rather than mid-conversation)
- #15545 (related — Create Skill Entry Point; similar guided-action surface, different scope)

title: [Feature]: Agent Conversation Work Mode — Coding vs Daily Work
body:
## Background

Cherry Studio Agent conversations render every tool call as a card in the message stream — tool name, status, parameters preview, and an expandable details section. Even though details collapse by default, the cards themselves occupy the conversation visually and feel "engineering-flavored". Users who run Cherry Assistant or non-coding agents for writing, research, planning, or general daily tasks report the chat looks more like a developer console than a normal AI conversation. Codex popularized a "Work Mode" toggle that lets users choose how much technical detail to surface, and users increasingly expect Cherry Studio to offer the same control.

## Goal

Users can switch each Agent conversation between Coding mode (full technical visibility, today's behavior) and Daily Work mode (chat-like experience with execution detail hidden), with sensible defaults per built-in agent.

## Spec

- Work Mode has exactly two options: **Coding** and **Daily Work**. User-configurable per Agent.
- Built-in defaults: Cherry Claw and other coding-oriented agents default to **Coding**; Cherry Assistant and general-purpose agents default to **Daily Work**.
- Coding mode is identical to today's rendering — tool calls appear as collapsible cards with parameters and outputs available behind a chevron.
- In Daily Work mode, tool call cards are not rendered in the message stream. While a tool is running, a single lightweight status line appears (e.g. "Searching…", "Reading file…") and is removed when the next AI text or final answer arrives.
- In Daily Work mode, thinking/reasoning blocks render as a pulsing "Thinking…" indicator only; no expandable thought content.
- Tool permission prompts (approval cards) and error states must remain fully visible in **both** modes — users never lose the ability to approve, deny, or see what went wrong.
- Work Mode is a presentation setting only — message and tool-call history is stored identically regardless of mode. Switching modes mid-conversation re-renders the whole stream under the new mode and never re-runs anything.

## Verification

- Create a new Cherry Assistant conversation → default mode is Daily Work; ask "summarize today's tech news" → user sees a single "Searching…" line while the agent runs, then the final summary; no Bash / Fetch / Read cards appear.
- Create a new Cherry Claw conversation → default mode is Coding; ask it to read a file → tool cards (Read, Grep, etc.) appear collapsed with chevrons, expandable to full parameters and output.
- In Daily Work mode, trigger a Bash failure (e.g. command returns non-zero) → an inline error message with enough context to understand what failed appears in the message stream (not silently dropped).
- In Daily Work mode, the agent calls a tool that requires approval → the approval card renders fully (tool name, parameters, allow/deny buttons), regardless of mode.
- Toggle Daily Work → Coding mid-conversation → previously hidden tool calls now appear as collapsed cards with full history; no tools re-execute.
- Toggle Coding → Daily Work mid-conversation → tool cards and thinking blocks disappear from the stream; user messages and final AI answers remain unchanged.
- Change Cherry Assistant's mode from Daily Work to Coding manually, restart the app → Cherry Assistant still opens in Coding mode (override persisted).
- On a Cherry Assistant conversation that produced 12 tool calls during a long task in Daily Work mode, opening the conversation later still shows the clean chat view with the original status lines reconstructed (or omitted entirely), not the 12 cards.

## Related

#15085 #15118

title: [Feature]: Keep System Awake During Agent Execution
body:
## Background

Cherry Studio Agent tasks routinely run for many minutes — and with Goal Mode and long-running autonomous agents on the roadmap, sessions lasting hours are imminent. When users walk away mid-task, the system's display sleeps and, on macOS especially, App Nap and full system sleep throttle or pause Electron renderer processes. Local Agents (running entirely on the user's machine) silently stall or fail. Users have to either keep manually moving the mouse, install third-party tools like Caffeine / Amphetamine, or use `caffeinate` from the terminal — all friction that doesn't belong outside the app.

## Goal

Users can enable a setting that automatically keeps the system awake whenever an Agent session is actively executing, so long-running tasks complete without interruption regardless of how long the user steps away.

## Spec

- New global setting under Settings → General (or Performance section): **"Keep system awake during Agent execution"** — toggle, default OFF.
- When enabled, Cherry Studio acquires a system-level wake lock the moment any Agent session enters the executing state, and releases it the moment all Agent sessions return to idle / complete / error / cancelled.
- The wake lock blocks both display sleep and full system sleep. Display dimming for screen-saver / battery-saving brightness reduction may still apply.
- The wake lock is scoped to **Agent execution only** — normal chat conversations, idle Agent sessions, and the app simply being open do not trigger it.
- A subtle status indicator surfaces the lock state when active (e.g. small icon in the app status bar or sidebar footer), so users know the system is being kept awake on their behalf.
- When the setting is OFF, Cherry Studio's power behavior is identical to today (no regressions, no implicit awake lock).
- The setting is global (not per-Agent or per-session), persists across app restarts, and works consistently on macOS, Windows, and Linux.

## Verification

- Enable the setting, start a Cherry Claw task that takes ~10 minutes (e.g. multi-file refactor), close the laptop lid or let display sleep timer elapse — task continues running and completes; checking after returning shows full output.
- With the setting disabled, run the same 10-minute task and let display sleep on macOS — on resume, the task is paused/stalled or has thrown a network/runtime error mid-execution.
- Start 3 Agent sessions concurrently with the setting enabled; cancel them one by one — the wake lock stays acquired while at least one is executing, and releases only when the last one ends.
- Open Cherry Studio with no Agent running, setting enabled → verify system can still sleep normally (lock is only acquired during execution, not just because the setting is on).
- Trigger an Agent error mid-execution → wake lock is released within seconds, not held until the user manually intervenes.
- Toggle the setting on, restart the app → setting remains on; behavior unchanged.
- Use macOS `pmset -g assertions` (or Windows `powercfg /requests`) while an Agent is running with the setting enabled — Cherry Studio appears in the assertions list; appears nowhere when no Agent is running or the setting is off.
- The status indicator appears when the lock is held and disappears within ~1 second of the last Agent ending.

## Related

#15634
